pages_convention: XML section and paragraph locators (jats_text) for the abstract (§0 ¶1) and captions (cited as printed, e.g. Fig. 3); the supplied XML text contains no body text, so body steps cite printed journal pages, which equal the PDF pages counted from 1 (p. 1-14)

entry.evidence: It is yet less well established how fold-thrust systems deform under multiple compressional stresses.

sequences.source_document: Ogawa & Back 2022, Tectonophysics 841, 229574 (PDF and XML text)

steps.action: Pose the question of how fold-thrust belts deform under multiple compressive stress components.
steps.quote: It is yet less well established how fold-thrust systems deform under multiple compressional stresses.

steps.action: Take the published mixed model as the working frame: gravity-driven contraction in the south and crustal-driven contraction in the north of the NW Borneo belt.
steps.quote: has been previously explained by compressive gravity-driven stresses in the south and crustal-driven tectonics in the north

steps.action: Select the transition zone between the two inferred segments, covered by an 8700 km2 industry 3D seismic merge (six surveys, 1990-2003) and borehole data.
steps.quote: we focus on an area at the transition between the inferred gravity-driven southern part

steps.action: Check the average velocity cube used for depth conversion against well-to-seismic ties.
steps.quote: The validity of the velocity cube for depth-conversion was confirmed by well-to-seismic ties in several wells

steps.action: Interpret nine seismic horizons, following a published horizon framework and ages, and 57 faults; measure fault orientations with Stereonet.
steps.quote: interpreted in total nine seismic horizons

steps.action: Establish two structural provinces (SW and NE domains) that differ in strike, thrust style, backthrusts and wavelength, and a boundary striking N70° (Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 4).
steps.quote: subdividing it into two structural provinces: the SW and NE domains

steps.action: Compare the domains with the published present-day borehole-breakout stress field (King et al., 2010); note that the NE structures are oblique to the present stress.
steps.quote: The SW and NE domains can be clearly distinguished by analysis of the current stress field

steps.action: Infer the timing of initiation and termination of each thrust from growth-strata and drape seismic facies (Fig. 6, Fig. 7): in-sequence from 10-9 Ma in the SW, area-wide at 9-7.3 Ma in the NE.
steps.quote: termination was mapped for each fault of the study area

steps.action: Cross-check the seismic-facies timing against the independent kinematic restoration.
steps.quote: These observations about thrust timing from seismic facies are also supported by kinematic restoration.

steps.action: Run 2D kinematic restorations (decompaction, fault-parallel flow, flexural-slip unfolding) on depth-converted lines orthogonal to strike to estimate shortening lengths and rates per domain (Fig. 8, Fig. 9).
steps.quote: revealed that the development of thrusts in each domain was kinematically distinct

steps.action: Estimate detachment depths, dips and taper angles from the restorations: landward-dipping, 3-5.4° taper in the SW; flat or seaward-dipping in the NE.
steps.quote: the transition area between the SW and NE domains of the study area is a meeting zone for different detachment levels

steps.action: Compare the detachment depths with the published area-depth-strain prediction of Carboni et al. (2019).
steps.quote: The interpreted detachment depths are consistent with the depth prediction based on the area-depth-strain method by Carboni et al. (2019)

steps.action: Take the finite-element expectation that the lateral gap between weak layers controls imbricate versus ramp-flat thrust style.
steps.quote: Feng et al. (2015) showed with a finite element model that frontal thrust systems evolve differently

steps.action: Match the observed detachment distribution to that expectation: patchy, separated detachments give imbricate thrusts in the SW; interacting detachments give ramp-flat thrusts in the NE.
steps.quote: these detachment surfaces connected to form a ramp-flat geometry sensu Feng et al. (2015)

steps.action: Take the critical-taper expectation that backthrusts favour low taper.
steps.quote: Backthrusting is more likely to occur with low taper, as explained by the critical taper wedge theory

steps.action: Compare the measured tapers with that expectation and explain them by differential sediment supply: near-zero NE taper with backthrusts against higher SW taper without them.
steps.quote: but it is lower in the NE domain almost down to zero

steps.action: Plot fold wavelength against stratigraphic thickness and compare with other shale-detached belts (Fig. 11); attribute wavelength to depocentre thickness rather than to domain.
steps.quote: a linear correlation between the fold wavelength and sediment thickness is also evident

steps.action: Compare thrust trends with candidate stress sources: SW trends parallel shelfal extensional faults; NE trends parallel the high-velocity-body edge, with overthrusts and onlaps at 9-7.3 Ma coinciding with peak NE thrusting (Fig. 5).
steps.quote: the thrust trend in the NE domain is generally parallel to the frontal edge

steps.action: List the published rival mechanisms for Late Miocene wrenching (oblique convergence, slab detachment uplift, Kinabalu granite, Sulawesi far-field stress) without discriminating among them.
steps.quote: The causes of wrenching and basement movement are still inconclusive

steps.action: Compare with the free-air gravity anomaly and shelf wrench faults (Fig. 13) to support basement-involved wrench transpression driving the NE domain.
steps.quote: The interpretation of basement-involved wrench tectonics is supported by a positive gravity anomaly

steps.action: Propose two explanations for the high-velocity body, compaction along the lateral ramp or carbonates, and leave both open.
steps.quote: may represent preferential rock compaction along the lateral ramp, or the occurrence of carbonate rocks

steps.action: Keep a dual-component contraction system: gravity-driven deformation in the SW and crustal-tectonic deformation in the NE, acting concurrently and independently.
steps.quote: was caused by a dual-component contraction system

steps.action: Refine the claim: a ca. 15 km interference zone, and the published NE-ward increase in crustal contribution reread as a change in the relative ratio of the two drivers (Fig. 3C).
steps.quote: Our results suggest that this spatial variation of the driving mechanisms towards the northeast is caused by the change in the relative ratio

steps.action: Compare with the Makran mixed system: there the driver changes perpendicular to strike, in NW Borneo parallel to strike.
steps.quote: In contrast, on the NW Borneo margin, the driving force changes parallel to the fold-thrust structures.

tree.answer: Yes: two structural provinces with distinct styles, trends and timing across the transition zone
No: structures and timing reconstructed from 3D seismic traces and growth strata
Explain the contraction drivers of the transition zone
Gravity-driven versus crustal-driven versus mixed; cited rivals for wrenching and for the high-velocity body
Partly: trend parallel to shelf faults versus to the high-velocity-body edge, and in-sequence versus pulsed timing
Found: past deformation known from seismic traces

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Partly: two domains in one belt; wavelength-thickness relation repeated across belts
Limited checks: timing cross-checked by restoration, detachment depths against a published method
Dual-component contraction system kept as best explanation
Not documented; no review file supplied

end.claim: Between the Late Miocene and Early Pliocene, the NW Borneo deepwater fold-thrust belt was driven contemporaneously and independently by gravity (SW domain) and crustal tectonics (NE domain), and the two mix only in a ca. 15 km interference zone.

decisive_move.sentence: Inferring per-fault thrust initiation and termination from growth-strata facies (Fig. 6, Fig. 7) shows the two domains deformed contemporaneously but with distinct timing and kinematics; without this step the dual-component claim would not exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the prior south-gravity / north-crustal model directed the choice of the transition zone (p. 2), but the data were legacy industry 3D surveys acquired 1990-2003 (p. 4). Claim: consistency checks only (timing against restoration, detachment depths against Carboni et al. 2019, trends against stress and gravity data); no decisive test that could have rejected the dual-component model. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: finite element modelling of decollement arrangement (via Feng et al. 2015), used as an expectation

novelty_claims.quote: We propose a dual-component contraction system as deformation driver for the NW Borneo deepwater fold-thrust belts
exhibits greater structural heterogeneity than deformation caused by a single-component compressive stress system

limits: The supplied XML text contains only the abstract and captions, so body quotes are copied from the PDF and cited by printed page. Supplementary Fig. S1 is cited but not supplied. The seismic data are confidential (p. 13), so no reproduction by others is possible. No explicit 'first' claim is made; the novelty entries are proposals. The restoration does not account for early layer-parallel shortening, so SE shortening may be underestimated (p. 4). The present-day stress obliquity in the NE domain is left open (stress change or transpression; p. 5). The causes of wrenching and the origin of the high-velocity body are unresolved. The wavelength-thickness relation is a sub-claim at regularity_in_range (p. 10); shortening amounts and detachment depths are sub-claims at estimate_with_resolution, but no uncertainties are given. Inference: the reviews by Elders and Cullen (p. 13) may have shaped the text, but no review file was supplied, so there is no review sequence. Inference: the Carboni et al. (2019) comparison involves a co-author (Back) and may not be fully independent.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Arbitrary restoration lines orthogonal to the structural trend

Gravity from induced uplift of the interior highlands
